title: Display and RGB LED: Output Isn't Only Movement
description: Component lesson. ACT doesn't always mean a motor. Sometimes the most useful thing a robot can do is simply show you something.

content.value: One RGB LED Is Really Three

You met a single-colour LED all the way back in Module 3. An RGB LED is the same idea, tripled: three tiny LEDs — red, green, blue — packed under one shared lens. Light them in different combinations and proportions, and your eye blends the three into a single perceived colour.

content.title: 🌈 Mix a colour
content.hint: Try setting all three sliders to 255 — then all to 0. Notice what those two extremes look like.

content.value: Full red, green and blue together reads as white to your eye — the same three-colour mixing your screen uses for every colour it shows you. All three at zero is simply off. Every other combination is somewhere in between.
A Display Is Just Many of These

The dot-matrix grid in the widget above isn't a separate idea — it's simply many controllable coloured lights arranged in a grid, each one a pixel, exactly the same way a camera's grid of light sensors works in reverse. A screen's job is to fill that grid, row by row, fast enough that your eye sees a stable picture instead of a scan happening.

one RGB LED         -->  one controllable coloured dot
grid of many         -->  a display
filled row by row,   -->  looks like a stable picture
fast enough

This is the direct mirror of Module 8's camera lesson: a camera's grid of sensors turns light into numbers; a display's grid of LEDs turns numbers back into light. Same grid idea, opposite direction — just like microphone and speaker.

Key takeaway: an RGB LED mixes red, green and blue light to produce any colour. A display is nothing more than a grid of controllable lights like this, filled fast enough to look like a stable picture.

quiz.question: What's actually inside a single RGB LED?
options: One LED that changes its own material to shift colour
Three separate tiny LEDs — red, green and blue — under one shared lens
quiz.explain: Colour mixing happens because your eye blends the light from three separate, independently controllable LEDs.

quiz.question: What colour does full red, full green and full blue together produce?
quiz.explain: All three primary colours of light at full strength mix to white — the same principle your screen uses for every colour.

quiz.question: How does a display relate to the camera lesson earlier in this module?
options: A display is the reverse of a camera's sensor grid — numbers becoming light instead of light becoming numbers, on the same grid idea
Displays don't use a grid at all
quiz.explain: Same grid-of-pixels structure, opposite direction of conversion — exactly like the microphone/speaker pair earlier in this module.
